{{nihongo|'''Kamisumuji Shrine'''|神須牟地神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Settsu Province]].

It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}}, and its former shrine rank was {{ill|Son-sha|ja|村社|qid=Q134917284}}. It is also called '''Kamisumuji-sha'''<ref name="Osaka city"/>.

== History ==
[[File:Kamisumuji-jinja history sign.JPG|thumb|250px|Origin board of the shrine.]]
The shrine history board states: "An ancient Engishiki-listed shrine called Sannomiya, founded nearly 2,000 years ago."

While {{ill|Sumiyoshi-taisha|Q705949|qid=Q705949}} was called the ichinomiya of {{ill|Settsu Province|Q864163|qid=Q864163}}, this shrine was regarded as the sannomiya{{Sfn|Osakajin|2010|p=39}}. In the Edo period, when daimyo worshiped at Sumiyoshi Taisha on sankin-kotai journeys, they were said to change from travel wear into prescribed formal attire at this shrine before worship{{Sfn|Osakajin|2010|p=39}}.

Priests of Sumiyoshi Taisha often concurrently served here, but after WWII, amid postwar disorder, this shrine faced a crisis of survival. A priest from an old shrine in {{ill|Yao, Osaka|Q490872|qid=Q490872}} accepted this shrine's land without charge and became its first guji{{Sfn|Osakajin|2010|p=39-40}}. The shrine's current origin text was researched and edited by his son, the second guji{{Sfn|Osakajin|2010|p=40}}<ref group="注釈">The current guji is the son of the second guji (grandson of the first); his second son is former {{ill|professional baseball player|Q11336312|qid=Q11336312}} {{ill|Keiji Obiki|Q6383649|qid=Q6383649}}.</ref>.

== Precinct ==
== Main shrine ==
Traditionally worshiped as a guardian deity of brewing and medicine, and known for strong divine virtue as a protector of both letters and arms.

The main shrine buildings were destroyed by war in the Keicho era, then rebuilt on August 21, {{ill|Windberg (Freital)|Q6811|qid=Q6811}} ({{ill|Genna|Q635245|qid=Q635245|lt=Genna}} 4) by cooperation of four people including the Toyotomi retainer Tagaya{{Sfn|Osaka Prefectural Shinto Youth Association|1971|p=76}}. In the ninth month of {{ill|1736|Q6989|qid=Q6989}} ({{ill|Genbun|Q1145754|qid=Q1145754}} 1), the Tokugawa shogunate, concerned that this shrine and Tamai Shrine were declining, had two stone markers erected via mountain-merchant Ibei Yamaguchiya (Sugano Hirofusa){{Sfn|Osaka Prefectural Shinto Youth Association|1971|p=76}}.

== Marker stone ==
This is one of marker stones set at 20 shrines that Edo-period Confucian scholar {{ill|Namikawa Seisho|Q6563872|qid=Q6563872}} identified as previously-lost {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} shrines. Shikinaisha are shrines listed in the ''{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}'' (volumes 9 and 10), many of whose locations became unclear with the dissolution of the ancient state system<ref name="Osaka city"/>.

In the Edo period, momentum rose to clarify and honor these shrines. From {{ill|1729|Q6952|qid=Q6952}} to {{ill|1735|Q6984|qid=Q6984}}, Namikawa compiled ''{{ill|Five Kinai Chronicles|Q11372555|qid=Q11372555}}'', identifying all uncertain Shikinaisha in the province with existing shrines. Due to cost, full-scale commemoration was difficult, so marker stones were first erected for 20 shrines in Settsu. This was carried out from {{ill|1736|Q6989|qid=Q6989}} into the following year with support of the Tokugawa shogunate, by Kubo Shigenobu under Namikawa's direction in Akagawa village (present {{ill|Akagawa|Q76140132|qid=Q76140132|lt=Akagawa}}, {{ill|Asahi-ku, Osaka|Q861271|qid=Q861271|lt=Asahi Ward}}). All markers still exist, four within Osaka City. Before Namikawa's identification, this shrine was called by another name, "Sannomiya." Although parts of his textual criticism are now seen as insufficient, these markers are important materials showing development of early-modern empiricism and antiquarianism<ref name="Osaka city"/>.
